title: Middle District Daily: November 25, 2026
notes_html:
Middle District of Florida employment decisions newly available on Westlaw
Episode length: 2 minutes 51 seconds

Dowling v. Stantec, Inc.
Case No. 8:26-cv-02284-MSS-LSG, Tampa Division, District Judge Mary S. Scriven, decided November 23, 2026
2026 WL 3590021
Breach of contract and Florida Private Whistleblower Act retaliation (pro se plaintiff). Result: motion to remand granted; case returned to the Sixth Judicial Circuit, Pasco County.

The removing defendants did not show by clear and convincing evidence that no contract claim was possible against the Canadian parent, whose joinder defeated diversity. A 2017 offer letter that reached "affiliated" companies, plus a 2020 TN visa support letter stating a higher salary to be paid by Stantec in Canada, left room for a modified agreement that binds the parent, despite an unrebutted defense declaration. The court noted that Florida courts have not addressed whether immigration representations can modify an employment agreement. It did not reach the whistleblower "employer" question and left personal jurisdiction to the state court as overlapping with the contract merits.

Deadline: None set. The case was remanded.

Practice point: One possible claim against the nondiverse defendant is enough, so lead with the cleanest one and attach the offer letter, affiliate definitions and visa support filings. Expect the employer and personal jurisdiction defenses to return in state court. Research for this episode found no Middle District decision treating lack of personal jurisdiction as fraudulent joinder. Persuasive authority from outside the district declining to decide personal jurisdiction on remand, on a different rationale and not cited in this order: Magdalena v. Toyota Motor Corp., 2013 WL 12092086 (S.D. Fla.); Liljeberg v. Continental Tire the Americas, LLC, 2012 WL 602306 (M.D. Ala.).

title: Middle District Daily: November 23, 2026
notes_html:
Middle District of Florida employment decisions newly available on Westlaw
Episode length: 4 minutes 33 seconds

Rusek v. Department of Homeland Security
Case No. 8:24-cv-2849-SPF, Tampa Division, Magistrate Judge Sean P. Flynn (on consent), decided November 20, 2026
2026 WL 3572122
Federal employee Title VII race and sex discrimination and Whistleblower Protection Act (pro se plaintiff). Result: government's motion to dismiss the amended complaint as a shotgun pleading denied.

A probationary USCIS asylum officer alleges a temporary supervisor pressured him to decide cases by her politics and that he was fired after he refused and reported her. The amended complaint stopped incorporating every prior count and split the race, sex and whistleblower claims into separate counts, and its dated chronology gave the government fair notice despite some conclusory lines. A stray reference to the already dismissed FCRA claim was treated as a drafting slip. Because the government raised no element-specific argument, the court declined to make one for it and expressed no view on whether any count states a claim.

Deadline: Defendants must answer within 14 days of the November 20, 2026 order.

Practice point: When the defense moves only on shotgun grounds, hold it to that motion; expect element challenges to return later.

Westlaw (subscribers)

Bowman v. R & R Industries, Inc.
Case No. 6:23-cv-02470-PGB-DCI, Orlando Division, Judge Paul G. Byron, decided November 19, 2026
2026 WL 3564059
FMLA retaliation. Result: amended motion for default judgment denied without prejudice.

The employer answered, went through Chapter 11, lost its counsel and was defaulted in June 2026. For the second time, the motion relied on the plaintiff's affidavit instead of citing the operative complaint. On default the court considers only well-pleaded complaint facts, so a renewed motion must tie each FMLA element to specific allegations in the complaint. The court relied on a consistent line of Middle District orders.

Deadline: Renewed conforming motion due on or before December 19, 2026, or the case may be dismissed for failure to prosecute.

Practice point: Brief default motions element by element with citations to complaint paragraphs; use affidavits for damages, not liability.

Westlaw (subscribers)

Gilmore v. NFC Amenities
Case No. 8:26-cv-1474-TPB-GDP, Tampa Division, Judge Tom Barber, decided November 17, 2026
2026 WL 3525346
ADA termination, failure to accommodate and unequal terms (pro se plaintiff). Result: unopposed motion to dismiss granted; amended complaint dismissed with prejudice; case closed.

The plaintiff again left the facts section of the court's form complaint blank after an earlier order explained what to add. With no factual allegations, there was no plausible claim, and a prior cure opportunity justified denying further leave to amend. The order says nothing about the elements of an ADA claim.

Practice point: At intake, a with-prejudice dismissal after a cure order like this likely ends the ADA claim.

Westlaw (subscribers)

title: Employee Rights Weekly: November 16 through November 22, 2026
notes_html:
Coverage: November 16 through November 22, 2026
Episode length: 17 minutes 15 seconds

Eleventh Circuit

Jones v. Franklin (School Board of Gadsden County)
11th Cir., unpublished, Nov. 16, 2026
No. 26-11227 (appeal from N.D. Fla. No. 4:25-cv-00188)
Westlaw: 2026 WL 3519448
Affirmed Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal of a pro se applicant's ADEA failure-to-hire and Title VII retaliation claims. A younger hire raised only on appeal was disregarded, with dictum that a younger hire alone would not suffice; retaliation failed for lack of any alleged decision maker knowledge, and a footnote treated a roughly two-year gap as too long.
Practice point: Plead the decision maker's identity and knowledge, and put replacement and comparator facts in the complaint. Expect the younger-hire dictum to be cited at the pleading stage.
Opinion (court) | Westlaw (subscribers)

Smith v. Emory Health, Inc.
11th Cir., unpublished, Nov. 12, 2026 (prior week, newly available on Westlaw)
No. 25-13093 (appeal from N.D. Ga. No. 1:23-cv-04314)
Westlaw: 2026 WL 3438516
Affirmed summary judgment on a physician's ADA retaliation and retaliatory hostile work environment claims. A modestly lower evaluation and a PIP were not materially adverse, given testimony they did not affect pay or promotion; suspension and non-renewal failed on pretext where the employer had good reason to believe she worked outside facilities and lied about it.
Practice point: Develop early evidence of what a PIP or review actually triggers inside the organization, and attack the investigation itself when the employer relies on its findings.
Opinion (Leagle) | Westlaw (subscribers)

Jackson v. Secretary of the Air Force
11th Cir., unpublished, Nov. 10, 2026 (prior week, newly available on Westlaw)
No. 25-10038 (appeal from N.D. Fla. No. 3:23-cv-03881)
Westlaw: 2026 WL 3408502
Affirmed summary judgment against a pro se federal employee on Title VII discrimination and retaliation claims, largely on abandonment, the 45-day EEO contact deadline, and reprisals that predated EEO contact. Restates the federal-sector 'any part' standard and treats the convincing mosaic as the ordinary summary judgment inquiry, with McDonnell Douglas as an additional route.
Practice point: Useful framework summary for federal-sector cases, but unpublished; check its significant-harm phrasing for retaliation before citing.
Opinion (Leagle) | Westlaw (subscribers)

Florida Appellate Courts

Lamb v. City of Tampa
Fla. 2d DCA, published, Nov. 13, 2026 (prior week, newly available on Westlaw)
No. 2D2025-0635 (review of PERC final order)
Westlaw: 2026 WL 3454429
Reversed PERC and directed it to order the City to promote a wartime-veteran officer. Section 295.09(1)(a) applies whenever a promotional exam is used; the eligibility list is the promotional register, and a discretionary final selection does not avoid the statute. Footnote 2 leaves open whether other criteria may shape eligibility or ranking; Judge Guard's concurrence would apply the preference at every stage.
Practice point: Ask every passed-over public-employee veteran whether an exam was used at any point. Press the every-stage argument and scrutinize when eligibility criteria were adopted.
Opinion (FindLaw) | Westlaw (subscribers)

Karac v. Fidelity National Information Services, Inc.
Fla. 2d DCA, published, Nov. 13, 2026 (prior week, newly available on Westlaw)
No. 2D2025-1811 (review of FCHR final order)
Westlaw: 2026 WL 3453782
Affirmed FCHR's dismissal of a pro se FCRA petition. No due process violation where the petitioner skipped the prehearing conference; remaining issues unreviewable on an incomplete record.
Practice point: Procedural reminder for the administrative hearing route: attend the prehearing conference and secure a complete record on appeal.
Opinion (FindLaw) | Westlaw (subscribers)

No Florida Supreme Court or DCA employment written opinion confirmed for November 16 through 22. Several employment-adjacent DCA dispositions that week were bare per curiam rulings with no written opinion. No employment-related rule amendments.

EEOC

American Medical Response to pay $2.2 million (Title VII religion and ADA)
EEOC, Nov. 16, 2026
D. Colo. Civil Action No. 1:22-cv-02544
Nationwide consent decree over a no-beard respirator policy that kept EMTs and paramedics with religious grooming practices or pseudofolliculitis barbae off the job, where an alternative respirator was available. Requires accommodation positions using that respirator and a study on expanding it.
Practice point: When an employer cites PPE or safety to refuse a grooming accommodation, ask what alternative equipment exists and whether it was considered.
EEOC release

All Inclusive Collection LLC to pay $45,000 (ADEA, Miami)
EEOC Miami District, Nov. 17, 2026
Conciliation (no lawsuit)
Miami employer's online job ad sought applicants under 40. A deterred applicant recovered about a year's pay, with policy changes, training and reporting of future postings.
Practice point: Screen age cases for deterred applicants and age-coded postings.
EEOC release

Prairie Green at Fay's Point to pay $160,000 (PWFA)
EEOC, Nov. 17, 2026
N.D. Ill. No. 1:25-cv-11111 (EEOC v. Blue Island SLF, LLC)
CNA with a lifting restriction was pushed onto unpaid leave and fired despite available vacant jobs she could temporarily perform.
Practice point: Clean example of temporary suspension of an essential function and forced-leave theories under the PWFA.
EEOC release

Tripp Enterprises to pay over $250,600 (sexual harassment, retaliation)
EEOC, Nov. 19, 2026
Conciliation (no lawsuit)
Nevada manufacturer resolves harassment, retaliation and constructive discharge charges of four women.
EEOC release

EEOC Fiscal Year 2026 Agency Financial Report
EEOC, Nov. 16, 2026
Reports $637.7 million recovered, mostly pre-litigation, and about 99,500 charges, up roughly 13 percent.
Practice point: Factor rising charge volume into client expectations on investigation timing.
EEOC release

No new EEOC guidance, technical assistance, rules or Commission votes this week.

Department of Labor

Final rule: employee or independent contractor status (FLSA, FMLA, MSPA)
DOL Wage and Hour Division, announced Nov. 19, 2026
RIN 1235-AA46; Docket WHD-2026-0001
Rescinds the 2024 six-factor test and returns to an economic reality test with two core factors, control and opportunity for profit or loss; skill, permanence and integration are less probative, and actual practice outweighs the contract. Says compliance, safety and quality-control requirements alone do not show employee status. Effective 60 days after Federal Register publication.
Practice point: Expect defendants to lead with the two core factors and the safety and compliance carve-out. Build the record on actual control and on whether profit depends on business judgment rather than hours.
DOL release | Rule text | Fact Sheet 13

Opinion Letter FMLA2026-3: off-hours work and travel count toward the 1,250 hours
DOL Wage and Hour Division, Nov. 17, 2026
FMLA2026-3
Required work outside scheduled hours, including at home, counts toward FMLA eligibility under the suffer-or-permit standard; travel between worksites likely counts. Without accurate records, the employer bears the burden to show the employee fell short, including for exempt employees.
Practice point: Use against 'not eligible' defenses for salaried employees whose employers track only scheduled hours.
Opinion letter

Opinion Letter FLSA2026-14: seasonal amusement exemption and food concessionaires
DOL Wage and Hour Division, Nov. 17, 2026
FLSA2026-14
A concessionaire inside an amusement or recreational establishment is part of it, so seasonality under section 13(a)(3) is measured for host and concessionaire together. Ordinary restaurants generally are not amusement establishments.
Practice point: Expect this in stadium, fair and seasonal-venue overtime cases; the restaurant point helps plaintiffs.
Opinion letter

EBSA release on Bolton v. Inland Fresh Seafood Corp. of America (en banc 11th Cir.)
DOL EBSA, Nov. 16, 2026 (decision Oct. 13, 2026)
Release No. 26-1640-NAT; 11th Cir. No. 24-10084
Westlaw: 194 F.4th 108
DOL, which appeared as amicus, praised the unanimous en banc ruling that ERISA does not require exhaustion of plan remedies for statutory claims such as fiduciary breach; the court overruled Mason v. Continental Group. Exhaustion still applies to benefit claims.
Practice point: Revisit statutory ERISA claims held for plan appeals and any pending motion relying on Mason.
DOL release | Westlaw (subscribers)

Proposed rule: PERM labor certification overhaul
DOL Employment and Training Administration, Nov. 16, 2026
Release No. 26-1607-NAT
Proposes longer and modernized recruitment and other changes to permanent labor certification; comments due in January. Little direct effect on employee-side litigation.
DOL release

No new Field Assistance Bulletins or OSHA whistleblower guidance.

NLRB

Trader Joe's East
NLRB, Nov. 19, 2026
375 NLRB No. 69; Case 13-CA-394913
Routine test-of-certification decision finding an unlawful refusal to bargain at a Chicago store. No doctrinal change.
NLRB case page

No new General Counsel memos or precedent-changing Board decisions.

Three things to watch or act on

  1. Review open misclassification and FMLA coverage matters under the new independent contractor rule; target discovery at actual control and real profit-or-loss opportunity.
  2. For salaried clients denied FMLA as ineligible, ask about off-hours and travel work and the employer's time records; FMLA2026-3 shifts the burden when records are missing.
  3. Screen public-sector intake for veterans passed over after a promotional exam; Lamb v. City of Tampa supports promotion as the remedy. Watch for employers rewriting rules around its footnote 2.

title: Middle District Daily: November 21, 2026
notes_html:
Middle District of Florida employment decisions newly available on Westlaw
Episode length: 8 minutes 14 seconds

Parke v. Delta Air Lines Inc.
Case No. 6:23-cv-2221-JSS-NWH, Orlando Division, Judge: JSS (docket initials), decided November 19, 2026
2026 WL 3561950
Florida Private Sector Whistleblower Act (FPSWA), plus negligent retention and defamation. Result: summary judgment for Delta; Parke's cross-motion denied; case closed.

A flight attendant fired in 2022 after a boarding dispute over masking claimed she was fired for objecting to Delta's COVID-19 rules for unvaccinated workers. Applying Gessner v. Southern Co., the court required proof of an actual violation of law by the employer, not just a reasonable belief. Her ADA medical-exam theory failed because the court relied on cases holding a COVID-19 infection is not an ADA disability. Her theory that a ramp agent and a manager interfered with crewmember duties failed because an individual employee's violation is not the employer's, and there was no evidence Delta ratified it.

Takeaway: An FPSWA claim needs an actual violation tied to the employer's own policy or practice, or proof the employer approved the conduct.
Westlaw (subscribers)

Louzada v. ME of Cape Coral North, LLC (Massage Envy)
Case No. 2:26-cv-1929-KCD-NPM, Fort Myers Division, Judge: KCD (docket initials), decided November 19, 2026
2026 WL 3561901
Title VII and FCRA sex discrimination, national origin discrimination, and retaliation (six counts). Result: motion to dismiss denied in full.

The only male therapist alleged fewer assignments, canceled appointments, missing tips, and repeated mocking of his accent, and he was fired three days after renewing a complaint. The court held a comparator is part of the McDonnell Douglas evidence framework, not a pleading requirement, and pretext arguments were premature. Repeated accent mocking was more than a stray remark, and he did not need to name each speaker. Informal complaints to supervisors are protected activity, and three days was close enough in time to plead causation.

Deadline: Defendant must answer within 14 days of the November 19, 2026 order.

Takeaway: A strong recent answer to motions that demand a comparator or proof of pretext at the pleading stage.
Westlaw (subscribers)

Deng v. Bladen Community College
Case No. 8:26-cv-02008-JLB-GDP, Tampa Division, Judge: JLB (docket initials), decided November 16, 2026
2026 WL 3513208
Title VII, FMLA, and breach of contract (pro se plaintiff). Result: motion granted in part; case transferred to the Eastern District of North Carolina, with no ruling on the dismissal arguments.

A math instructor at a North Carolina college sued in Tampa after he was fired, noting he was allowed to finish end of semester duties from Sarasota. The court held Title VII's own venue provision, 42 U.S.C. 2000e-5(f)(3), controls over the general venue statute. The decision makers and records were in North Carolina, and he would have kept working there. Where the plaintiff was when he got notice of the firing does not matter.

Deadline: Clerk directed to transfer the case and terminate all deadlines.

Takeaway: For remote or relocated workers, check Title VII's venue statute before filing in Florida.
Westlaw (subscribers)

Tortora v. Manny's Cucina Napoletana LLC
Case No. 6:25-cv-00877-JSS-LHP, Orlando Division, Magistrate Judge Leslie Hoffman Price, decided November 17, 2026
2026 WL 3539532
FLSA overtime and retaliation against a restaurant and two individuals. Result: motion for default judgment denied without prejudice.

All three defendants defaulted, but each count was pleaded against a single unnamed "Defendant" while the plaintiffs sought joint liability against all three, which the court flagged as a possible shotgun pleading. The motion also did not address individual or enterprise coverage. The court doubted that restaurant work and handling food that moved in commerce would establish coverage on their own.

Deadline: Within 21 days of the November 17, 2026 order, plaintiffs must file a standalone renewed motion for default judgment or a second amended complaint, or the court will recommend dismissal without prejudice.

Takeaway: Even on default, plead each count against each defendant and prove FLSA coverage with facts.
Westlaw (subscribers)

Edwards v. Elevance Health, Inc.
Case No. 6:26-cv-01925-CEM-LHP, Orlando Division, Magistrate Judge Leslie Hoffman Price, decided November 18, 2026
2026 WL 3547851
Title VII sex and race discrimination and retaliation, and Equal Pay Act (pro se plaintiff). Result: employer's motion to stay discovery denied.

The employer argued the Title VII claims were untimely and the Equal Pay Act claim was poorly pleaded. After a preliminary look, the court was not convinced the motion to dismiss would end the whole case, and the employer conceded it might only narrow it. General claims of cost and burden did not justify a stay.

Takeaway: A pending motion to dismiss rarely pauses discovery in this district unless it clearly disposes of the entire case.
Westlaw (subscribers)
